prime.problem: Sampling k programs once and checking whether any passes gives a noisy 0 or 1 per task. Scoring code by text similarity rewards look-alikes over working code. You need an execution-based number that is stable enough to compare models.
prime.fits: First concept card. It is the metric the whole paper holds fixed. The Codex paper introduced it; here the question is what happens to it when the tests behind "correct" get stricter.
prime.goal: Compute pass@k from n and c, explain what the estimator is averaging over, and explain why stricter tests lower it by lowering c.

attend: What event does C(n−c, k) / C(n, k) measure the probability of, and why is pass@k one minus it?
Why draw n = 200 samples when you only want pass@10?
HumanEval+ changes neither the model nor the samples. Which symbol in the formula does it change?
Why are a model's pass@1 and pass@100 usually reported at different temperatures?
What does pass@100 quietly assume you can do with 100 programs?

must: Draw n samples, count c that pass every test → the chance a random k-subset has no correct sample is C(n−c, k)/C(n, k) → pass@k is one minus that → an exact expectation instead of a noisy single draw
Correct is defined as "passes every test" → stricter tests turn some of the c passing samples into failures → c drops → pass@k drops, with the same model and the same samples

Larger k only needs one success among k → it rewards diversity → best temperature rises with k → pass@1 and pass@100 are measured at different settings, and pass@100 assumes you can pick the right program
elevated: pass@1★ uses one greedy sample, not the estimator → it is 0 or 1 per task, averaged over 164 tasks → deterministic, but it can't give pass@10 or pass@100

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3–4 sentences what pass@k estimates, how the closed form gets it from n and c, and why HumanEval+ lowers it without touching the model.
checklist: probability that at least one of k samples passes every test
draw n ≫ k, count c, and use 1 − C(n−c, k)/C(n, k) (the chance k random picks all miss)
averaged over tasks; best temperature per k reported
stricter tests lower c, so pass@k falls with identical samples
pass@1★ is the separate greedy, single-sample number

retrieve.q: Explain why the unbiased estimator is preferred to drawing exactly k samples and scoring 1 if any passes.
answer: one draw of k gives 0 or 1 per task: high variance
n = 200 samples and the closed form give the exact expected value over all k-subsets
same cost per sample, far less noise

retrieve.q: Walk through the worked example's k = 2 row: which two numbers you divide, what that ratio means, and how you get 0.533.
answer: C(7, 2) = 21 ways to pick 2 from the 7 wrong samples
21/45 is the chance both picks are wrong

retrieve.q: A team reports pass@100 = 90% and says their model "solves 90% of tasks". What is the catch, and when would pass@1 be the honest number?
answer: pass@100 counts a task solved if any of 100 attempts passes
you only get that in practice if you can pick the correct one (your own tests or a ranker)
with one shot and no selection, pass@1 (or pass@1★) is what users see

compare.q: Both papers use the same estimator with n = 200. What is each paper using pass@k to measure, and what does each treat as fixed?
answer: Codex: compares models and sampling settings; the tests are fixed
EvalPlus: models and samples fixed; the tests change
same formula, different lever: Codex moves the model's c, EvalPlus moves the definition of "correct"

compare.q: BLEU and pass@k both score generated code against something the benchmark provides. Which design choice makes pass@k track correctness, and how does each metric fail?
answer: BLEU compares text to a reference; pass@k executes against tests
BLEU fails on equivalent code written differently, and on near-identical but wrong code
pass@k fails when the tests are too weak: exactly this paper's finding

predict.q: One task has n = 10 samples and c = 3 pass HumanEval's tests. HumanEval+ adds an input that one of those 3 fails, so c = 2. Commit first: does pass@5 fall by more or by less than pass@1, in absolute points and relative to where each started?
predict.answer: Absolute: pass@5 falls more (0.917 → 0.778, 0.139) than pass@1 (0.300 → 0.200, 0.100). Relative: pass@5 falls less (about 15% vs 33%). High-k scores are cushioned because one surviving correct sample still rescues most k-subsets, but the curve is steep in the middle, so the absolute loss can still be larger. That's why the paper quotes relative drops for different k.

apply.task: Keep going from the prediction. With n = 10 and c = 1, compute pass@1, pass@2 and pass@5 and add the row under the card's c = 3 row and the c = 2 row (0.200, 0.378, 0.778). Then write one sentence on how pass@5 collapses as c goes 3 → 2 → 1, and why a single correct sample still gives pass@5 = 0.5.
apply.done: c = 1 gives 0.100, 0.200 and 0.500. Your sentence says that with one correct sample, exactly the 5-subsets containing it pass, and that is 5 of the 10 samples' worth: C(9, 4)/C(10, 5) = 126/252.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the absolute drop or the relative drop?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why n = 200 when k is at most 100?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: stricter tests → lower c, or lower c → lower pass@k?
Could you explain to a non-ML engineer why pass@100 flatters a model?
What will you look for in the HumanEval card: where the tests that decide c come from?
